packages.title: Aquarium Summer Heat, Low Oxygen & Power Outages — Fact-Checked Research Packet for NotebookLM and Podcast Development
packages.document_date_notes: Cover says 'Prepared July 2026'. PDF metadata creation date is 2026-07-13.
main_topics: Dissolved oxygen solubility and temperature ('thermal oxygen squeeze')
Temperature and fish metabolism / oxygen demand
Surface agitation, gas exchange, and aeration
Low-oxygen warning signs (non-diagnostic)
Cooling methods: fan/evaporation, reducing heat input, frozen bottles, cooler small water changes
Ammonia speciation (NH3 vs NH4+) with pH and temperature
Feeding during extreme heat
Power outages and emergency aeration
Storm and blackout preparation, including pre-staged water
Temperature controllers and alerts (INKBIRD as brand example)
packages.core_message: In summer heat, do not focus on temperature alone. The dangerous squeeze is that warmer water can hold less dissolved oxygen while fish and other aerobic life may demand more oxygen.
intended_use: Source document for NotebookLM when developing the next Tank Guide Life podcast episode (not a verbatim script).
Separates well-supported science from practical hobby guidance and calls out claims that need cautious wording.
Fact-check of The Tank Guide's summer aquarium heat article (editorial baseline).
Sources section intended for NotebookLM citations and follow-up source tracing.

evidence_framework_used.summary: Section-level 'Research basis: S#' citations, a Claim Audit that assigns a fact-check status to each article idea, a 'Claims to Avoid or Soften' table with verdicts, stated source-prioritization rules, and explicit research limitations.
evidence_framework_used.citation_convention: Each research section ends with 'Research basis: S#, S#'. Figures carry 'Source: S#'. Sources are numbered S1–S16 in Section 14.
evidence_framework_used.source_prioritization: Sources were prioritized toward U.S. government agencies, university extension/aquaculture guidance, a peer-reviewed review, recognized fish-research guidance, emergency-preparedness agencies, and official product documentation. Commercial aquarium blogs were not used as scientific authorities.

claim_audit.editorial_note: Do not assign a universal doubling rate.

claim_audit.editorial_note: EPA and NRCS describe turbulence/agitation as enhancing atmospheric oxygen transfer.

claim_audit.editorial_note: Reasonable aquarium application of the supported aeration principle.

claim_audit.article_idea: A fan can cool an aquarium through evaporation.
claim_audit.editorial_note: Do not promise a fixed temperature drop.

claim_audit.article_idea: A sealed frozen bottle can be used for emergency cooling.
claim_audit.editorial_note: Monitor temperature and avoid abrupt swings.

claim_audit.article_idea: A slightly cooler small water change may help lower tank temperature.
claim_audit.editorial_note: Condition source water and avoid drastic temperature change.

claim_audit.article_idea: Higher pH and temperature increase the fraction of total ammonia present as NH3.
claim_audit.editorial_note: EPA 2013 document provides the chemistry relationship.

claim_audit.article_idea: Feeding less can reduce waste and post-feeding oxygen demand.
claim_audit.editorial_note: Do not create a universal fasting rule.

claim_audit.article_idea: Battery-operated air pumps are useful in outages.
claim_audit.editorial_note: Backup aeration aligns with aquatic life-support contingency guidance.

claim_audit.article_idea: Manual scoop-and-pour agitation can temporarily promote gas exchange.
claim_audit.editorial_note: Agitation supplies aeration; treat as a temporary stopgap.

claim_audit.article_idea: Pre-filled aquarium water can help before a forecast blackout.
claim_audit.editorial_note: Use clean covered dedicated containers and frame as short-term storm prep.

claims_to_avoid.better_wording: Higher temperatures can increase metabolism and oxygen demand; the response varies by species and conditions.

claims_to_avoid.tempting_claim: Air-stone bubbles do not add any oxygen.
claims_to_avoid.better_wording: Aeration works through circulation, turbulence, surface renewal, and gas transfer; focus the listener on surface movement.

claims_to_avoid.tempting_claim: A fan will lower the tank 2°F to 5°F.
claims_to_avoid.better_wording: A fan can cool through evaporation; the amount depends on humidity, airflow, surface area, and room conditions.

claims_to_avoid.tempting_claim: Lower a HOB tank exactly one or two inches.
claims_to_avoid.better_wording: Slightly lower the level enough to increase surface disturbance while keeping the filter operating properly.

claims_to_avoid.tempting_claim: Do the scoop-and-pour method every hour for several minutes.
claims_to_avoid.better_wording: Repeat periodically and respond to fish behavior; tank demand varies.

claims_to_avoid.tempting_claim: Stop feeding all fish during a heat wave.
claims_to_avoid.better_wording: Consider feeding less during extreme heat and watch water quality.
Higher pH and temperature can shift a greater fraction of existing total ammonia toward toxic NH3.

claims_to_avoid.tempting_claim: Loose ice is dangerous because cold itself is toxic.
claims_to_avoid.better_wording: Avoid untreated ice and uncontrolled temperature swings; use monitored, gradual cooling.

claims_to_avoid.tempting_claim: Every blackout needs a water change.
claims_to_avoid.better_wording: Prepared water gives you options; use testing and tank conditions to decide.

research_limitations: Aquaculture pond and research-facility sources are used for underlying water chemistry, aeration, physiology, and life-support principles. A home aquarium is a smaller system, so practical application should remain cautious.
Species-specific safe temperatures are intentionally not generalized. The podcast should tell listeners to know the temperature requirements of the exact livestock they keep.
No universal dissolved-oxygen emergency threshold is proposed for all aquarium fish. Species and life stages differ.
No universal manual-aeration interval is proposed. A small, heavily stocked warm tank can decline differently from a large, lightly stocked aquarium.
Product features are model-specific. INKBIRD is a brand example, not a claim that every INKBIRD controller has the same alarms, connectivity, or outputs.
Prepared water advice is short-term storm readiness, not a blanket recommendation for indefinite storage.

packages.core_message: Each of the three parameters answers a different question — pH: how acidic is the water right now; GH: how much calcium and magnesium is dissolved; KH: how much acid the water can absorb before pH moves. Knowing one tells you very little about the other two; knowing all three tells you a great deal.
packages.core_message_notes: Paraphrased from Section 4.1 ('The Core Insight'), which the package calls the integration point of the document. The package states that 'No editorial conclusion is drawn about what a podcast episode should say', so this is recorded as the document's central organizing insight, not an editorial verdict.
intended_use: A research reference compilation, 'not an article, not a script, and not a narrative'; it exists to serve as a retrieval corpus (Purpose and Scope).

Written for machine retrieval first and human reading second: terminology repeated deliberately, synonyms stated explicitly, conclusions close to evidence, intentional redundancy, uncertainty labeled (Purpose and Scope).
Ingestion into NotebookLM as a retrieval corpus for podcast and content development; not intended for direct publication (Document Notes).
Compiled as source material for Tank Guide Life, a production of FishKeepingLifeCo (cover).

evidence_framework_used.summary: Every substantive claim is intended to carry a claim-level evidence tag from a nine-category Evidence Classification Key; the bibliography is separately grouped by evidentiary tier (seven source tiers); Section 32 applies a six-level classification scale to 34 hobby claims; several sections carry their own verdicts or evidence summaries. The package also states up-front source-reliability problems (circular hobby citation; fabricated citations) and a rule for how numbers are sourced.
evidence_framework_used.citation_convention: Inline parenthetical author–year or title citations (e.g., '(Wurts & Durborow, 1992, SRAC 464)', '(Merck Veterinary Manual, Environmental Diseases of Aquatic Animals in Aquatic Systems)', '(Duarte, Smith, Val & Wood, 2016, Scientific Reports 6:20377, DOI 10.1038/srep20377)'). There are NO numeric or S# source keys and no numbered bibliography. Some bibliography entries carry parenthetical annotations stating what they were used for. Several in-text mentions name only an organization (e.g., 'Merck') or a body of work ('Gonzalez, Wood, Wilson, Val and colleagues … see the bibliography').
evidence_framework_used.original_source_key_convention: Because the package uses no source numbering, each source's original_package_key.key in this registry is the bibliography entry's own author–year (or organization + title) label, and original_package_key.bibliography_entry_verbatim preserves the full entry text. bibliography_tier and bibliography_tier_position record where the entry sits in the package's tiered bibliography. No registry-invented keys (such as S1) are assigned.

claim_evidence_classification_key.source: About This Document — Evidence Classification Key (p. 7)
claim_evidence_classification_key.instruction_verbatim: Every substantive claim in this document is intended to fall into one of the following categories. Where a claim is not explicitly tagged, its category should be inferred from the surrounding language (“established,” “commonly reported,” “anecdotal,” etc.).

tags.label: Established scientific principle
tags.meaning: Textbook chemistry or physiology; not seriously disputed

tags.label: Strong evidence
tags.meaning: Multiple peer-reviewed studies or authoritative agency consensus

tags.label: Reasonable inference
tags.meaning: Sound extrapolation from established principles to the aquarium case, but not directly tested in aquariums
tags.example: Therefore a heavily stocked, rarely-changed aquarium will lose KH over time

tags.label: Aquaculture / fisheries practice
tags.meaning: Standard commercial or agency practice, well documented, but usually developed for ponds/RAS rather than glass aquariums
tags.example: Liming ponds to raise alkalinity above 20 mg/L

tags.label: Common aquarium practice
tags.meaning: Widely used by hobbyists, plausible mechanism, limited formal testing
tags.example: Crushed coral in a filter bag

tags.label: Anecdotal observation
tags.example: “My shrimp colony crashed after a large water change”

tags.label: Contested claim
tags.example: Whether a 1.0-unit pH change is inherently dangerous

tags.label: Unsupported or misleading folklore
tags.meaning: Repeated widely; mechanism absent, backwards, or overstated

source_reliability_problems_stated.summary: A very large fraction of aquarium care-sheet content is copied from other care-sheet content; when the document reports a 'commonly cited range', that means commonly cited, not empirically validated (About This Document, p. 7; see Section 30).

source_reliability_problems_stated.problem: Problem 2: Fabricated or unverifiable citations on aquarium content sites.
source_reliability_problems_stated.summary: Multiple recently published aquarium websites were found citing specific-sounding studies that could not be located in any indexed literature database; these claims are not reproduced as facts anywhere in the document (About This Document, p. 7; Section 36.14; Sources Deliberately Excluded).

evidence_framework_used.numeric_claim_rule_verbatim: Consequence for this document: where a number is given, this document either (a) cites a traceable authoritative source, (b) shows the arithmetic derivation, or (c) explicitly labels the number as a hobby convention of unknown provenance.
evidence_framework_used.evidence_handling_verbatim: claims are tagged by evidence tier throughout. Where credible sources disagree, the disagreement is documented rather than resolved. Where a commonly repeated figure could not be traced to a primary source, it is labelled as hobby convention.
hobby_conventions_flagged_by_package: 'Never change pH more than 0.2 per day', '0.3 per day' and '1.0 is deadly' — could not be traced to a controlled study (Sections 6.4, 32 Claims 14–16).
Raise GH ~1–2 dGH per week (Section 11.4) and KH no more than ~1–2 dKH per day (Section 13.3) — convention rather than validated science.
Shrimp TDS/GH/KH targets — hobby convention, provenance not traceable to primary research (Sections 26.5, 28.3).
'Never change TDS by more than 20 ppm at once' — convention without traceable evidentiary basis (Section 26.6).
Snail shell minimum of roughly 6+ dGH with pH not persistently below ~7.0 — hobby convention (Section 28.5).
Ca:Mg target of roughly 3:1 to 4:1 — practitioner consensus; evidence for a specific optimum is weak (Section 11.3).
Aquasoil lifespan ranges — hobby-reported, not manufacturer specifications or measured data (Section 18.3).
Specific drip rates ('2 drops per second') — convention, not evidence (Section 31.6).
research_limitations: The physiological literature cited is weighted toward Amazonian and temperate model species, because that is where the research exists. Southeast Asian, Central American and African species are less well covered by ionoregulation research.
Very little controlled research exists on the “thriving” tier for ornamental species (Section 8.5). Much of what the hobby believes about long-term effects of chronic parameter mismatch is inference.
Manufacturer dosing figures are reproduced as manufacturer claims and were not independently verified.

Specific numeric thresholds widely used in the hobby (rate-of-change limits, shrimp TDS targets, snail GH minimums) are labelled as conventions because their provenance could not be established. This should not be read as evidence they are wrong — only that they are unverified.
evidence_framework_used.research_limitations_source: Document Notes — 'Known limitations of this document' (p. 94), transcribed verbatim.
